prompt.context: Your client is the sugar cereal division of Foods Inc., a U.S.-based distributor and manufacturer of packaged foods. Foods Inc.'s traditional strength has been with grocery stores, which still account for the majority of its $1.1 billion in sugar cereal sales. Big M Mart, a discount chain, has been growing at a healthy rate of almost 15 percent per year and has now become Foods Inc.'s largest customer. Your client is not sure how to react, and has asked BCG for assistance with its distribution strategy.
prompt.question: How should Foods Inc. react to Big M Mart's growth and what should be its distribution strategy going forward?

clarifying_info.q: How do grocery stores differ from discount stores?
clarifying_info.a: Grocery stores generally specialize in food, as well as selling some household goods and over-the-counter pharmaceuticals. Discount stores offer food alongside a wide variety of merchandise, including clothing, home electronics, and housewares.

clarifying_info.q: Does Big M Mart market its food products differently than grocery stores?
clarifying_info.a: Discount stores advertise lower prices for a wide variety of foods, particularly staple, nonperishable foods.

exhibits.title: Sales and Volume by Top 5 Distributors (1997-2001)
exhibits.shows: A table of Foods Inc. sugar cereal sales (in $M) and volume (in million boxes) broken out by the top 5 distributors and totals for 1997, 1999, and 2001, along with the 5-year CAGR for each distributor.

framework: 1. Channel performance: Compare Foods Inc. sales and margins across distribution channels, with focus on Big M Mart vs. other channels
2. Competitive analysis: Assess Foods Inc. market share vs. competitors specifically within the Big M Mart channel
3. Customer behavior: Understand what drives purchase decisions (brand loyalty, price sensitivity, impulse buying, shelf placement)
4. Supply chain: Analyze distribution process, stock-out frequency, and inventory visibility at store level

questions.prompt: What does the sales and volume data tell us about Big M Mart as a distribution outlet and about Foods Inc.'s margins there?
questions.guidance: Big M Mart is the fastest-growing distributor by both sales (14.7% CAGR) and volume (14.7% CAGR). Critically, for Big M Mart the sales CAGR equals the volume CAGR, meaning the average price per box has stayed flat — unlike other channels where sales growth exceeds volume growth. This implies Big M Mart is not paying more per box over time, putting downward pressure on margins relative to other channels. Big M Mart now exceeds 21% of total sugar cereal revenue ($246M of $1,150M in 2001).

math.setup: Compare sales CAGR vs. volume CAGR for each distributor to infer pricing trends. Calculate Big M Mart share of total revenue in 2001.
steps: Big M Mart sales CAGR = 14.7%; volume CAGR = 14.7% => average price constant
R.J.'s sales CAGR = 6.2%; volume CAGR = 4.2% => price rising in that channel
math.answer: Big M Mart holds ~21% of total revenue and is the fastest-growing channel, but flat price-per-box suggests lower or non-improving margins vs. other channels.

questions.prompt: How would you find out how Foods Inc. is doing versus competitors within Big M Mart, and what does the market share data show?
questions.guidance: Approach: interview Big M Mart purchasing personnel by offering to share consumer insights and identify joint cost-reduction / revenue-increase opportunities. Market share data shows Foods Inc. and Tasty Breakfast losing share, while Cereal Co. and Private Label are gaining. Cereal Co. is the main threat. Private Label is growing from a small base.

questions.prompt: What explains Cereal Co.'s market share gains at Big M Mart?
questions.guidance: Price competition has been avoided industry-wide after price wars 6-7 years ago. Shelf space is equal (30% each for name brands, 10% private label). However: Cereal Co. products are placed lower on shelves (important for children, the key target demographic); Cereal Co. has in-store promotion tags and is advertised in store flyers for cardholders; Cereal Co. dedicates 50 sales reps to the Big M Mart account vs. Foods Inc.'s 7. The greater sales force investment explains better placement, promotional cooperation, and growing share.

questions.prompt: Given the consumer research findings, what are the implications for Foods Inc.'s strategy at Big M Mart?
questions.guidance: 60% of buyers are brand-loyal (go straight to their preferred cereal) — availability/stock-outs are the critical driver for this group. 40% are impulse buyers (survey all options then choose) — shelf placement and promotion matter for this group. Consumers are not generally price-sensitive unless a stock-out of their preferred brand occurs, at which point 35% will buy a discounted cereal, 25% will walk away without any purchase, and 40% will act like impulse buyers. Product availability is therefore a key success factor.

questions.prompt: Quantify the sales impact of the 15% stock-out rate at Big M Mart stores.
questions.guidance: Calculate the proportion of total purchase occasions lost because brand-loyal customers walk away empty-handed.

math.setup: 15% of cereal SKUs are out-of-stock. 60% of customers are brand-loyal. When a brand-loyal customer hits a stock-out, 25% walk away without buying anything.
steps: Lost purchase occasions = 15% (stock-out rate) x 60% (brand-loyal share) x 25% (walk-away rate)
math.answer: Stock-outs cause Foods Inc. (and Big M Mart) to lose approximately 2.25% of potential cereal sales from brand-loyal customers who simply walk away.

questions.prompt: How is Foods Inc.'s product currently distributed to Big M Mart, and what are the supply chain implications?
questions.guidance: Cereals are delivered from factory to distributor warehouse twice monthly. Big M Mart then stocks shelves itself. Foods Inc. has no visibility into in-store inventory or stock-out events at individual stores. Given that product availability is a key success factor, Foods Inc. must work to gain real-time in-store inventory data from Big M Mart.

brainstorming.prompt: What recommendations would you make to Foods Inc. regarding its distribution strategy with Big M Mart?

categories.name: Partnership and relationship investment
ideas: Increase dedicated sales reps focused on the Big M Mart account (from 7 toward the 50 that Cereal Co. deploys)
Propose a formal joint business planning process with Big M Mart
Offer to share consumer behavior research (brand loyalty data, stock-out impact analysis) as a value-add to Big M Mart

categories.name: Distribution and availability improvements
ideas: Negotiate access to Big M Mart's real-time store-level inventory data to detect stock-outs proactively
Explore more frequent or direct-to-store delivery options to reduce stock-outs
Collaborate with Big M Mart to improve shelf replenishment processes and timing
Understand root cause of current 15% stock-out rate before investing in solutions

categories.name: Shelf placement and in-store promotions
ideas: Negotiate for shelf placement at child eye-level (matching or beating Cereal Co.)
Develop joint promotional programs (store flyers, loyalty cardholder specials) similar to Cereal Co.'s
Explore end-cap or secondary placement opportunities

categories.name: Channel mix and margin management
ideas: Assess whether Foods Inc. is accepting Big M Mart's pricing pressure or has room to push back
Work with grocery channel partners to ensure they can remain competitive
Evaluate whether incremental Big M Mart volume at flat margins is dilutive or accretive to overall profitability

categories.name: Competitive response
ideas: Monitor Cereal Co. promotional activity and respond with equivalent or superior programs
Understand whether Cereal Co. has an exclusive arrangement with Big M Mart or whether Foods Inc. can replicate similar terms
Evaluate the private label threat and decide whether to supply private label or defend branded share

recommendation: Foods Inc. should pursue a deeper partnership with Big M Mart rather than pulling back, because Big M Mart is the fastest-growing channel (14.7% CAGR) and now represents over 21% of total sugar cereal revenue — walking away or deprioritizing it is too costly.

The immediate priority should be to solve the stock-out problem: stock-outs cost both Foods Inc. and Big M Mart ~2.25% in lost sales; resolving them creates a clear economic case for Big M Mart to share in-store inventory data and accept more frequent replenishment.

Foods Inc. must dramatically increase its sales force dedicated to Big M Mart (currently 7 vs. Cereal Co.'s 50) to improve product placement, secure promotional slots, and build the relationship needed to compete on equal terms with Cereal Co.
risks: Sales through Big M Mart carry flat or declining margins (price per box not growing); investing more to grow this channel could reduce overall profitability if pricing is not renegotiated.
Foods Inc. does not yet understand the root cause of the 15% stock-out rate or the cost to eliminate it — investing in distribution improvements without this diagnosis could be wasteful.
Big M Mart may continue to favor Cereal Co. if a deeper relationship already exists — Foods Inc. may not be able to replicate Cereal Co.'s terms.
Devoting significant resources to Big M Mart could weaken Foods Inc.'s service to grocery channel partners, who still represent the majority of $1.1B in revenue.
next_steps: Conduct root-cause analysis of the 15% stock-out rate and estimate the cost of remediation.
Negotiate access to Big M Mart's store-level POS/inventory data.
Benchmark Foods Inc.'s Big M Mart margins vs. grocery channel margins to quantify the profitability trade-off.
Develop a proposal for Big M Mart offering joint consumer research and improved distribution in exchange for better shelf placement and promotional access.
Build a business case for increasing the Big M Mart sales force from 7 to a level competitive with Cereal Co.
